analysis.one_liner: Requires electric utilities to offer community solar so renters can buy solar power.
analysis.headline: A one-senator bill to require every electric utility to offer community solar — letting renters and apartment dwellers buy solar power without a rooftop — was referred to the Senate Energy Committee in June 2025 and has seen no action since, with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require every electric utility to offer a "community solar" program — a shared solar project whose electricity credits are subtracted from subscribers' utility bills. That would let people who cannot put solar panels on a roof (renters, apartment dwellers, and low- and moderate-income households) buy into solar for the first time. It also directs the Department of Energy to help states, tribes, and local governments design these programs, and to open existing DOE loan and grant programs to community solar projects.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters, apartment dwellers, and low- and moderate-income households who cannot install rooftop panels would gain a way to subscribe to solar and offset their electric bills. Solar developers and community-solar companies would gain a guaranteed nationwide market of subscribers, and utilities would be allowed to own facilities too. State, local, and Tribal governments would get federal technical help building programs.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every electric utility that is not a Tribal utility to offer a community solar program to which all ratepayers — including low-income ratepayers — have "equitable and demonstrable access," so renters and people without suitable rooftops can buy solar power through their existing utility bill.

Directs the Energy Department, within one year of enactment, to set up a program to expand community solar access for individuals without regular access to onsite solar, particularly low- and moderate-income people, and to align it with existing federal programs serving low-income communities.

Orders DOE to give states, local governments, and Tribes technical help designing affordable rate structures and financing models, and to use the National Laboratories to publish data that helps private entities finance and run community solar projects.

Expands existing DOE grant, loan, and financing programs to cover community solar, and extends the maximum federal contract term for public utility services from 20 to 30 years, making long-term solar subscription contracts possible for federal facilities.

analysis.who_pays: Electric utilities would bear the cost of building and administering community solar programs, some of which would likely be recovered through rates paid by all customers. State regulators and nonregulated utilities must run proceedings to consider the new standard within one year and finish within two. The bill authorizes no new spending, so the DOE program would depend on future appropriations.

drawbacks.text: The federal "standard" only forces states and utilities to consider community solar, not adopt it: under the bill's own compliance language, a state regulator or nonregulated utility can hold a hearing and then decide the standard is not appropriate, so a hostile state could satisfy the law by rejecting it.

Utilities' program costs would likely flow back into rates for all customers, including people who never subscribe, and the bill sets no guardrails on what subscribers may be charged beyond a requirement for equitable access.
The bill authorizes no money for the DOE program it orders up, so its technical-assistance and financing promises would depend entirely on future congressional appropriations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households priced out of rooftop solar, community solar subscriptions typically shave a real amount off monthly electric bills, and a national utility mandate with an explicit low-income access requirement would be a meaningful consumer gain at a modest, diffuse cost spread across utility ratepayers. The bill's main weakness is that it is a mandate to consider, not a mandate to adopt — states can reject the standard after a hearing — and it comes with no dedicated funding, so its reach would depend on how each state and utility implements it.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Luján introduced the bill on June 26, 2025, and the Senate sent it to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor ever since.

narrative.text: Senator Ben Ray Luján introduced the Community Solar Consumer Choice Act of 2025 on June 26, 2025.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day; that referral is the last action of any kind on the bill.
No senator has signed on as a cosponsor, and the committee has held no hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it pending while the 119th Congress continues.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the status quo holds: utilities and their state regulators face no requirement to offer community solar, and the solar industry gets no new federal mandate. Renters and lower-income customers who might have subscribed gain nothing yet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo; utilities face no new requirement

sides.party_line_note: No vote has occurred and no one has opposed the bill on the record; the only signal is that a lone Democrat sponsored it and not a single senator from either party has cosponsored it.

industries.industry: Community solar developers and solar installers
industries.note: A requirement that every utility offer a community solar program would create a large new subscription market for solar developers. The bill tries to keep that market open by requiring ownership mechanisms for utilities, subscribers, and third parties alike and by directing national-lab data to help private financing.

Utilities would have to build and administer community solar programs and open them to all ratepayers, a real compliance burden they could partially recover through rates. But the bill also lets utilities own community solar facilities and gives states the option to reject the standard after a hearing, softening the mandate.

Community solar subscriptions offset utility bills with solar generation, shifting some electricity demand away from conventional generation if programs scale. The bill does not target fossil plants directly.

analysis.trajectory: With a single sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no committee action months after referral, the bill is on the standard path to quietly dying in committee at the end of the 119th Congress. Its realistic route forward would be folding its community solar provisions into a larger energy package that the Energy and Natural Resources Committee actually advances; on its own it is very unlikely to reach the floor.
